analysis.one_liner: Narrows the law letting foreign victims sue in U.S. courts over torture, slavery, and genocide.
analysis.headline: The bill drew zero cosponsors, was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, and received no further action before the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have rewritten the Alien Tort Statute, a 1789 law that lets non-citizens sue in U.S. federal courts for serious violations of international law. It would have limited the claims a victim could bring to six categories — torture, extrajudicial killing, genocide, piracy, slavery, and slave trading — and required that the defendant be a direct participant acting with specific intent. It would also have let the President block any such lawsuit with a written certification that it hurt U.S. foreign policy, barred suits against foreign states acting in their own territory, banned contingency-fee arrangements, and imposed a 10-year filing deadline. The bill never left the Judiciary Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Multinational corporations and other defendants facing lawsuits by foreign victims of human-rights abuses. Requiring 'direct participation with specific intent' would have effectively ended cases built on aiding-and-abetting or corporate-complicity theories, where a company is accused of enabling a government's abuses rather than committing them directly. The presidential certification power, the exhaustion requirement, the ban on contingency fees, and the strict pleading and timing rules would each have made it harder for victims to sustain a case.
analysis.who_benefits_short: U.S. companies sued over overseas abuses

how_it_helps.text: Limits actionable claims to six categories: torture, extrajudicial killing, genocide, piracy, slavery, and slave trading, removing other claims courts had entertained under the open-ended statute.
Requires every defendant to be a 'direct participant acting with specific intent,' which excludes liability theories based on aiding and abetting or corporate complicity.
Bars jurisdiction over suits where a foreign state committed the abuse within its own sovereign territory.
Allows the President (or a designee) to stop any case by certifying in writing that proceeding would harm U.S. foreign policy interests.

Requires victims to first exhaust remedies in the country where the injury occurred, imposes a 10-year filing deadline, bans contingency-fee arrangements, and mandates detailed factual pleadings with discovery stayed during motions to dismiss.
Makes federal district court jurisdiction original and exclusive, centralizing these cases in one court system.

analysis.who_pays: Victims of torture, slavery, genocide, and other abuses committed or enabled by corporate actors abroad, who would have lost their main route to a hearing in an independent court. People harmed in countries where local courts are unavailable or controlled by the same government would bear the heaviest burden, since the bill requires exhausting 'adequate and available' local remedies first.

drawbacks.text: A victim suing a company accused of complicity in forced labor or killings would have to prove the company directly participated with specific intent — a standard most complicity cases could not meet, effectively closing the courthouse door even for well-documented abuses.

The President could kill any pending or future case with a written certification of foreign-policy harm, giving the executive branch unilateral power over individual victims' lawsuits with no judicial check beyond the certification being 'adequate.'
Requiring victims to exhaust remedies in the country where they were abused can be impossible in practice when that country's courts are controlled by the regime accused of the abuse.
The ban on contingency fees would prevent victims with no money from hiring counsel, since these cases typically proceed on that basis.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Defenders of curbing the Alien Tort Statute argued that courts were stretching a 1789 law to reach modern corporate conduct abroad, producing decades-long, speculative suits against companies whose connection to the abuse was indirect, and creating friction with foreign governments. The bill addressed those concerns but went far beyond them: the specific-intent requirement, the presidential kill switch, and the contingency-fee ban together would have shut out most victims with genuine claims, not just weak ones. The protection it offered industry came almost entirely at the expense of abuse survivors with few other legal options.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, where it sat with no cosponsors, no hearings, no markup, and no floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Dianne Feinstein introduced the bill in the Senate on October 17, 2005, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary.
The bill had zero cosponsors, according to the Congress.gov cosponsor page.
The full action history shows no activity after the referral — no committee report, no hearing listed, no vote — and the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007, without the bill advancing.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died in committee, victims of torture, slavery, and genocide retained the broader ability to sue in U.S. courts under the unamended Alien Tort Statute, and the multinational corporations that would have gained a shield did not get one.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Victims who kept access to U.S. courts

for.name: Dianne Feinstein
for.role: U.S. Senator from California and sole sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Alien Tort Statute Reform Act on October 17, 2005 and delivered introductory remarks on it.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee (109th Congress)
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on October 17, 2005 and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no report — before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No votes ever occurred and the bill had zero cosponsors, so no member other than the sponsor's support is on record either way.

industries.industry: Multinational corporations with overseas operations (oil, mining, apparel, and similar industries)
industries.note: These companies were the main defendants in Alien Tort Statute cases alleging complicity in torture, forced labor, and killings abroad. The bill's direct-participation-and-specific-intent standard, presidential override, and procedural hurdles would have made such suits nearly impossible to bring or win.

The bill bans contingency-fee arrangements in these cases, which is how most human-rights victims afford representation, and imposes strict pleading rules with discovery stayed during dismissal motions.
